name: ISLANDERS - translucent radius preview sphere before placing
one_line: When you pick up a building to place, a translucent sphere appears around the cursor showing exactly which existing buildings/terrain are within scoring range before you commit
take_what: Show the influence radius as a live overlay attached to the cursor/ghost tile DURING placement (not after), so the player sees which enemy/friendly tiles will be affected before committing - directly attacks Limen's 'placement lacks strategic feeling even though math exists' problem

name: boards.faeria.com - How to Improve at Faeria (J0k3se guide)
one_line: High-level player guide diagnosing why games drag: passive defenders overspend resources holding position instead of counter-attacking, plus a concrete land-placement rule to force early contact
take_what: Concrete rule: place your first lands closest to the OPPONENT's base/orb (not defensively in front of your own), which denies them a free summon-and-swing turn and forces them to spend resources on defense from turn one - this is the actual mechanism that prevents corner-turtling

name: Connection Games III: Havannah and Starweb (Dr Eric Silverman)
one_line: Breaks down Havannah's three simultaneous win conditions (ring, fork, bridge) and Starweb's triangular-number scoring that rewards a 'minority strategy' of raiding instead of hoarding corners.
take_what: Havannah forces players to threaten and defend three different win shapes at once, which is what keeps placement tense across the whole board instead of players building safely in a corner. Concretely: Starweb's score formula rewards CONNECTED clusters superlinearly (n+(n-1)+...+1), which makes turtling in one corner strictly worse than contesting multiple fronts - directly answers Limen's 'players build up in their own corners' problem.

name: Marvel Snap: The Definitive Deconstruction
one_line: Deconstructor of Fun's full teardown of Marvel Snap: 6-turn/~4-minute matches, locations revealed progressively turns 1-3, and the Snap/retreat escalating-cube-wager mechanic (1-2-4-8 stakes)
take_what: the Snap mechanic: either player can double the match's stakes at any point, opponent must choose retreat/continue/counter-snap - this FORCES a confrontation decision every single turn instead of letting both sides quietly build in their corner, which is exactly Limen's problem 1 (slow-start, no early interaction)
constraint: none - abstract wager mechanic, not IP-locked

name: Neuroshima Hex: Battle Review (Meeple Mountain)
one_line: Reviewer's take on why the tension-then-release structure of Battle-token triggering feels like real combat
take_what: Board fills silently over many turns with zero interaction (a 'cold and calculated' placement phase) until ONE Battle tile ends the turn immediately and detonates every armed tile at once - the whole game's violence is deferred into a single player-chosen instant, not distributed turn by turn

name: Bumbling Through Dungeons - King of Hill in Combative Board Games
one_line: Essay analyzing Kemet, Inis, and Time of Crisis on how contested-center scoring must reward the fight OFFENSIVELY (build toward your own win) not just defensively (deny the leader), or players avoid the center entirely.
take_what: Warning: if attacking the center-holder is purely punitive ('you're not doing anything positive toward your own ends'), players skip the fight and turtle - contested zones need the attacker to gain something concrete (VP, resource, tempo) from the act of contesting, not just deny the defender
constraint: none - direct design-problem-1 relevance: explains WHY current Limen corner-turtling happens if capturing enemy tiles has no independent upside beyond denial

name: Arcs Designer Diary 3 - The Trick's the Thing (Leder Games)
one_line: Cole Wehrle's diary on why Arcs uses trick-taking as its core action-selection system, explicitly to fight the multiplayer-solitaire tendency of Eurogames
take_what: Lead/Follow action economy: on your turn you either play a HIGH card to seize the lead action (fewer total actions that round) or a LOW card to let someone else lead but you and everyone get MORE actions - the whole table is forced to react to whichever card the leader shows, every single turn, because it decides what action is even available that round

name: Balatro: Juicy Feedback in a Poker Roguelike (sequential joker activation)
one_line: How Balatro visualizes joker-chain causality without any text
take_what: Jokers trigger left-to-right in a visual pulse sequence, each one bounces and the running score total updates immediately after each individual trigger (~300ms per step) - causality is taught by watching the chain fire, not by reading a log

name: Carcassonne tempo-blocking (road splitters, city-completion denial)
one_line: Players deliberately place tiles that make an opponent's feature harder to close, forcing them to spend future turns fixing it instead of expanding, or trap an opponent's follower in a feature that will never complete
take_what: A placement whose entire value is denial - it does nothing for your own board state, it only removes a completion path or traps an enemy resource in a dead feature - is a first-class strategic option, not a side effect
constraint: Limen already has some denial via capture-at-zero, but pure tempo-blocking (a placement with zero offensive value, purely to deny an enemy combo) is a distinct design lever worth naming explicitly to solve slow-start problem

name: Dorfromantik - quest tiles as demands placed ON the board
one_line: Objectives (e.g. 'close a forest region of 15 tiles', 'deer needs 3 connected forest tiles') are physical tokens sitting on specific hexes on the board itself, not a sidebar checklist
take_what: Bind the goal state to a literal board location so the player's eye and hand are pulled toward it while placing - the quest IS the map, not a UI panel next to the map

name: Duelyst mana tiles force center-board contact
one_line: 3 one-time-use mana tiles (top row, middle, bottom row) grant +1 mana for the turn when a unit moves/summons onto them, and are consumed permanently on first use.
take_what: A scarce, one-shot resource bonus placed at contested center squares that both players are magnetically drawn toward turn 1-2 — not a repeatable resource, so it front-loads the fight for center territory instead of letting players farm their own corner.

name: On the Value of Sente (Nordic Go Dojo)
one_line: Explains sente (initiative-forcing move) vs gote, and models the value of sente as the point-gap between alternating descending move values (e.g. 4,3,2,1 -> sente worth 2 points net).
take_what: A concrete forcing-move economy: rank available plays by 'threat value', and whoever holds initiative always grabs the current-highest-value play while the responder is stuck answering. Give Limen tiles an explicit 'forcing' flag (like siege/menace) that obligates a same-turn-or-next-turn response, and track who is spending turns responding vs. who is choosing freely - surface this as a visible 'initiative' indicator.

name: Marvel Snap (Second Dinner)
one_line: Mobile CCG, hard 6-turn match cap, 12-card no-duplicate decks, mid-game doubling-cube 'Snap' bet mechanic
take_what: Hard 6-turn cap with escalating per-location energy (turn N gives N mana) means every turn is 1/6th of the game and mid-game already has 6 mana of tempo swing available - forces early interaction because there's no 'build up in a corner for 10 turns' runway

name: Riftbound TCG (League of Legends card game)
one_line: Physical/digital TCG where 1v1 matches are won by racing to 8 points scored only by conquering (taking a battlefield you don't already control) or holding (controlling one at the start of your turn) contested battlefields.
take_what: Score points ONLY from contested/enemy-adjacent territory, never from your own uncontested corner: 'conquer' = take a zone you didn't control this turn (1pt), 'hold' = still control it at start of next turn (1pt). This makes turtling in your own zone worthless - you MUST cross into contested ground to score at all.
constraint: none - abstract scoring pattern, not proprietary content

name: The Four Core Pillars of Marvel Snap Strategy ("Marvel Snap Is Four Other Games")
one_line: Strategy essay breaking Marvel Snap's early/mid/late/wager decisions into four distinct sub-games happening on one board
take_what: locations act like poker community cards: only 1 of 3 locations is visible on turn 1, the other two reveal on turns 2 and 3 - so the first moves are forced bets under incomplete information rather than safe corner-building, and revealed-vs-unrevealed slots create asymmetric risk/reward for committing early

name: Neuroshima Hex: Battle - A Deep Dive into Strategic Gameplay (Opinionated Gamers)
one_line: Review/analysis of the initiative-ordered simultaneous battle resolution and Battle-token turn structure
take_what: Combat resolves in initiative tiers, highest-initiative units act first each tier and can kill lower-initiative units before those units ever act - 'you will know if they are saving one for future use' since all drawn tiles are face-up, making Battle-token bluffing a known-information mind game, not hidden info

name: Hey, That's My Fish!
one_line: Penguin tile-grab game where every move removes the tile you left, permanently shrinking the board and cutting off routes.
take_what: Moving off a tile REMOVES it from the board immediately (not on a timer) - your own movement is what shrinks the map, so every turn both gains territory and destroys it, forcing early pathing decisions and cutting opponents off from regions before midgame
constraint: none - simple mechanic, public design pattern

name: Clash Royale — Double Elixir & Overtime Sudden Death
one_line: Real-time card/tower hybrid where the last 60s of a match doubles resource regen and adds a first-hit-wins overtime, with 3x elixir in the final overtime minute
take_what: Elixir regen rate literally doubles (2.8s/pt -> 1.4s/pt) for the final third of the match, then triples in overtime; over 40% of matches are decided in this compressed window because both players can suddenly afford aggressive plays they were saving up for
constraint: none - pure numeric mechanism, not IP-bound

name: Marvel Snap is a testament to the power of ruleset design (Keith Burgun)
one_line: Designer essay dissecting why a 1-power creature on turn one in Snap is 'a huge deal' while turn-one plays in Hearthstone are forgettable
take_what: Only 4 slots per lane x 3 lanes = 12 total board slots in the whole match, so each placement consumes a visible, scarce fraction of total game space - contrast with open hex grids where early tiles vanish into empty space

name: Landfall (MTG, Zendikar)
one_line: Triggered ability that fires any time a land enters the battlefield under your control - rewards an action nearly every deck already performs every turn
take_what: the design principle (Rosewater rates it 2nd-best mechanic ever): reward the ROUTINE action players take anyway rather than requiring a new resource. For Limen: since every turn already places exactly 1 tile, attach a small escalating bonus to 'placement count this turn/game' (e.g. every 3rd tile placed triggers a free micro-effect) so the core loop itself feels like it's paying off, addressing the 'placement lacks strategic feeling' problem directly

name: Duelyst general mechanic + small 9x5 board
one_line: Each player's General starts on the board at 25 HP on a compact 9-row-by-5-col grid; kill the enemy General to win instantly.
take_what: A single always-vulnerable win-condition unit (General, 25 HP) starts ON the board from turn 1, not behind a wall of setup — every unit summoned near it is simultaneously an attacker and a threat to the win condition, so aggression is never 'wasted' tempo.

name: Hive (Yianni, 2001) - core ruleset
one_line: Randomness-free abstract tile-laying game about surrounding the opponent's queen using bug-specific movement constraints, no board.
take_what: the One Hive rule: no move may ever split the connected mass of tiles into two groups, and no placed piece may ever be isolated - every single placement/move is filtered through this global connectivity check
constraint: none - public domain mechanic, not IP-protected rule text

name: The Battle of Polytopia — Pixelated Playgrounds design analysis
one_line: Design breakdown of Polytopia's compression: 16x16 map, ~5-turn exploration window before first contact, single 'stars' currency for everything
take_what: Hard map-size-to-player-count ratio that guarantees first contact within ~5 turns regardless of skill — the map isn't 'small for flavor', it's sized so exploration necessarily runs out before turn 5-6. Translated to Limen: shrink playable hex radius or force starting positions closer so first adjacency-contact between decks happens turn 2-3 instead of players building uncontested for 5+ turns

name: Summoner Wars 2E - Beginner's Guide
one_line: New-player strategy primer covering unit tempo, gate blocking, and the 3-action turn economy
take_what: explicit design principle: 'most units, especially commons, have their biggest impact on the turn they are summoned' - the game is built so holding cards is a trap, not a strategy, because fresh units get an immediate move+attack; also 'if your unit is adjacent to an opponent's gate, they cannot summon to that spot' making gates contestable board objects, not just static resources

name: Marvel Snap developer talks smart card game design (GamesHub interview, Kent-Erik Hagman)
one_line: Designer interview on why Snap's tight ruleset (6 turns, 12 cards, 3 lanes) produces deep decisions from turn one
take_what: Match length is a hard structural constant (exactly 6 turns, +1 mana/turn, max 4 slots per lane) rather than an open-ended race to a life total, so every single placement is legible against a known countdown

name: Discover (Hearthstone)
one_line: Effect shows 3 randomly-selected cards (from a filtered pool) face-up, player picks exactly one to keep/play
take_what: 3-option forced-choice-from-random-pool structure: designer Ben Brode's stated reason it feels great is that random pool + player pick is 'a random effect that adds skill' because the choice among 3 is fully informed even though which 3 appear is random - directly applicable to Limen's rift-drain or tile-draw randomness to convert bad-luck-feeling RNG into skill-expression RNG

name: Dorfromantik - Perfect Placement scoring & chime
one_line: Tile that matches all 6 edges triggers a distinctive audio chime plus a 60-point bonus and an extra tile added to your draw stack
take_what: A single sharp, distinct sound effect reserved ONLY for the rarest best-case placement (perfect 6-side match), contrasted against otherwise calm ambient audio, PLUS a tangible reward (extra card/tile) not just points

name: Tak rules - stack movement and carry limits
one_line: In Tak, a stack's top piece controls ownership; a move can pick up and 'carry' up to (board-size) stones from the top of a stack and drop them one-per-hex along a straight line, redistributing control as it goes.
take_what: A carry-and-drop movement mechanic for stacks: instead of static towers, let a max-3 tower in Limen 'unstack' by moving its top N tiles in a line to adjacent hexes, redistributing influence bonuses as it goes. This turns tower-building from a purely defensive stat-stack into an offensive maneuver with real board-shape consequences - directly targets Limen's 'placement lacks strategic feeling' problem by giving stacks a use beyond sitting still.
constraint: Tak's exact carry/drop rule is IP of Cheapass Games/James Ernest - implement the underlying idea (top-controls-ownership, redistribute-on-move) with different exact numbers

name: Into The Breach is at its best when it puts you into unwinnable situations (MCV/DEVELOP)
one_line: Design piece arguing ITB's best moments come from forced trade-offs with no clean optimal answer
take_what: For ~9 of 10 turns there is no dominant move - every turn is a forced trade between two named costs (e.g. 'save this building' vs 'save mech durability'), achieved by stacking a secondary objective (protect the dam/train) on top of the primary threat so resources are always overcommitted

name: Neuroshima Hex Rulebook PDF (Portal Games)
one_line: Official rulebook - primary source for the exact battle resolution algorithm and HQ shield rules
take_what: Battle resolves in strict initiative-tier passes (all tiles at initiative 3 attack simultaneously, then all surviving/undamaged tiles at initiative 2, etc.) rather than one-at-a-time - this tiered-simultaneous resolution is what lets a single Battle token detonate the whole board in one dramatic beat instead of a slow attack queue

name: Balatro strategy - joker synergy stacking (TheGamer)
one_line: Balatro's optimal builds combine one flat-chip joker + one scaling-mult joker + stacked x-mult jokers for multiplicative escalation
take_what: Two-axis multiplicative scaling (additive 'chips' layer times a separately-stacking 'x mult' layer) makes early plays feel small and late-run plays feel explosive off the same base numbers - Limen's effective-influence is purely additive (base+adjacent-friendly-adjacent-enemy); adding a rare multiplicative keyword/rite that multiplies a tower's stacked influence instead of adding would create the same escalation curve without changing base math

name: Connection Game overview - Wikipedia
one_line: Surveys the connection-game genre (Hex, Havannah, TwixT, Y, Slither) and the shared design principle that connection games avoid draws by construction and reward contesting shared, contested cells rather than building in safe isolated regions.
take_what: The genre-level design axiom that a connection game's win condition should make EVERY empty cell matter to both players simultaneously (no cell is 'purely mine' until claimed) - the opposite of Limen's current corner-building pattern where early tiles are placed with no opposing stake in them. Concretely: a scarce-resource overlay (e.g. only N total 'capital-adjacent' or rift-adjacent hexes exist) that both players are pulled toward from turn 1 would force early contact.

name: Neuroshima Hex!
one_line: Hex-tile army-building duel on a small board where drawing a specific 'combat initiation' tile forces an immediate, board-wide resolution of all adjacent conflicts.
take_what: A rare drawable tile type ('battle/net tile') that FORCES combat resolution the instant it's placed, rather than combat being continuously live - creates spikes of forced confrontation on a deliberately tiny board (small hex count = knife-fight-in-a-phone-booth) instead of relying on board size alone to force proximity

name: BGG search summary - Summoner Wars 2E design overview & event-card combo tech

name: Kingdomino 'blessing in disguise' draft-order coupling
one_line: Designer Bruno Cathala: picking the best tile this round costs you first pick next round (numbered tiles = pick order), so power and turn priority are always in tension with no external balancing needed
take_what: Couple 'strength of thing you take' directly and mechanically to 'your priority/agency next turn' - a single self-balancing lever (tile value = next pick order) replaces any hand-tuned catch-up mechanic

one_line: Explains the Snap/Cube doubling-stake mechanic: either player can double the match's stakes at any point, escalating risk and forcing a bluff/read minigame mid-match
take_what: A player-triggered stake-doubling action (Snap) that either player can invoke on their own turn, visible to the opponent immediately, converts a slow accumulation game into a bluffing/escalation minigame layered on top of the base ruleset - a cheap addable subsystem, not a rules rewrite

name: Cascade (MTG)

take_what: the exact procedure: reveal cards face-up until first eligible hit, cast it free, then resolve original spell - the 'free extra thing happened' feeling comes from stacking a mini-event INSIDE the resolution of a normal action rather than as a separate turn phase

name: God-Pharaoh's Gift combo deck (MTG Pioneer/Modern)

For Limen's 'no wow moment' problem: design 1-2 rare tiles/rites that convert accumulated board state (stacked towers, captured tiles) into one explosive turn-ending effect, rather than only incremental influence math

name: Duelyst positioning-is-a-game-in-itself (community strategy analysis)
one_line: Strategy essay on Duelyst openings: center tiles have maximum 'reach' (adjacency to future plays), so board position itself has value independent of card stats.
take_what: Explicit 'reach' framing: a tile's value = how many future placement options it opens up, not just its immediate stat bonus. Isolated/cornered placement is bad even with good numbers because it forecloses future adjacency plays.

name: Faeria Academy: Chapter 2 - Land Placement
one_line: Official strategy guide defining three named land-building archetypes (Rush/Mid-Range/Control) tied directly to which tiles you place and where
take_what: Naming and codifying archetypes purely by PLACEMENT pattern (e.g. 'pump prairies down the center' = rush, 'take the two side wells' = control) rather than by card contents - the board geometry itself is the deckbuilding axis players read and counter-play against

name: Faeria - Battlefield structure (Fandom wiki)
one_line: Describes the empty hex board with two orbs on opposite sides and four wells placed off-center, meaning the board is built fresh each match rather than pre-populated

name: Moyo (Go term) - GoMagic + AllAboutGo
one_line: Moyo is a loose framework of stones that projects influence over open space but is not secured territory; conventionally valued at ~50% of its eventual territorial worth until enclosed, and is always subject to invasion/reduction.

This gives corner-building players a soft incentive to actually contest rather than just stack influence numbers passively - turns the existing influence math into a felt spatial claim.

name: Carcassonne meeple scarcity (7 meeples across 70-90 tiles)

take_what: Hard cap of a small placeable-resource pool (7 meeples) shared across a much larger tile-draw pool, so 'do I commit here' is a real question on most turns, not just 'where do I place'

name: Gwent tribal row-adjacency boost (Dwarf/Scoia'tael archetype)

name: Dorfromantik - retroactive perfect-fit double-scoring

take_what: Scoring resolves not just for the tile placed but re-checks and rewards neighbors that just became 'complete' as a side effect - creates a cascade/chain-reaction feeling from one placement

name: Duelyst 'Replace' mulligan-any-turn mechanic

name: Developing Tak (Crab Fragment Labs, James Ernest)

constraint: none - direct numeric-tuning lesson (keep the meter short) is the reusable part

name: Matt Leacock's Forbidden Island series design diary
one_line: Designer diary on the Forbidden Island/Desert/Sky/Jungle series explaining he wants each shrinking-board sequel to visually communicate danger at a glance - 'oh wow, I can see you're all in danger' - even to onlookers.
take_what: Design goal: the hazard state must be legible to a passive observer, not just the players tracking numbers - shrinking/hazard visuals (sand dunes piling, tiles vanishing) are deliberately exaggerated beyond what's mechanically needed so danger reads instantly, which speaks directly to Limen's problem 2 (placement lacking strategic FEELING despite correct math)

name: TFT targeting mechanics roundup (search synthesis, sourced from Tacter/Mobalytics)
one_line: Catalog of non-default targeting patterns (nearest, farthest, lowest-HP-in-range, furthest-from-center) that individual champions use to break the frontline/backline default
take_what: varied targeting rules per unit type (nearest / farthest / lowest-effective-influence-in-radius) turn positioning into a rock-paper-scissors meta instead of one dominant strategy — e.g. a hypothetical 'flank' keyword unit that must capture the farthest-placed enemy tile rather than the weakest one would force spread-out defense
constraint: Limen already has flank/menace keywords per the brief; this suggests giving 1-2 more keywords an explicit TARGETING RULE (must capture farthest, or lowest-influence-in-2-hex-radius) rather than just a stat modifier

name: Marvel Snap Snap mechanic (doubling cube for stakes)
one_line: Backgammon-style doubling cube: either player can 'Snap' to double match stakes (cubes) mid-game, forcing opponent to retreat or commit
take_what: A mid-match player-triggered stakes-doubling button that converts a felt-advantage into a real commitment decision each turn - creates a 'wow, do I go for it' moment independent of the underlying board math

name: Slay strategy: hold Barons, build peasants for territory first
one_line: Player strategy consensus: cheap units to grab/hold land and grow income first, only upgrade to expensive units once economy can sustain the upkeep
take_what: The correct opening is NOT 'build your strongest piece' but 'grab cheap land fast because income scales with owned-hex-count' — expansion IS the economy, not a precursor to it. Directly counters corner-turtling because sitting still means a rival out-expands your income base

name: Defender's Quest — Optimizing Tower Defense for Focus and Thinking (Lars Doucet)
one_line: Design essay arguing tower defense should reward strategic THINKING over twitch reflexes via total time control (pause + variable speed) and total information (full stat readouts, wave preview)
take_what: Resource/cooldown costs are the only thing stopping pause-and-plan from being degenerate — action economy, not reaction speed, is what makes placement decisions feel weighty; pairs with full pre-battle visibility of what enemies/waves are coming so choices are informed, not blind

name: Designing MARVEL SNAP (GDC 2023 talk)
one_line: Ben Brode's GDC talk on building Marvel Snap around a fixed 6-turn match and Backgammon's doubling cube
take_what: the game was explicitly built around the 'double it' gambit from Backgammon (the Snap/Cube wager) as the primary hook, not bolted on after the core loop was done - wager mechanic came before card design

name: Adapt (Hearthstone, Journey to Un'Goro)
one_line: Pick 1 of 3 randomly-drawn keyword upgrades (from a fixed pool of 10) to attach to a minion already on board
take_what: applies Discover's 3-choice structure to BOARD STATE not hand/deck - designer Dean Ayala's stated design rule: adaptations only ever buff the minion itself (never draw/damage) so the 'story' stays legible. For Limen: a tile-placement or capture event could trigger 'pick 1 of 3 keyword buffs to slap on a placed tile' making placement itself a mini-choice-point instead of a flat number

name: What is wrong with Duelyst (a follow-up article) — Mivvv's Blog
one_line: Community critique: heavy randomness (Sirocco, Chrysalis Burst, etc.) undermined the tactics-game promise, and 'SMOrc' face-rush minion swarms became the dominant degenerate strategy despite positional design intent.
take_what: Anti-pattern warning: positioning depth erodes when random-effect cards or raw stat-stacking swarms let players skip the spatial puzzle entirely (win by volume, not placement). For Limen, any keyword/rite that lets a player bypass adjacency math (blind AOE, pure stat pump) should be capped or costed higher, or it will hollow out the influence-math feel the same way.

name: Stalk's Videogame Corner: Faeria (Cubic Creativity)
one_line: Retrospective review analyzing Faeria's turn-dial action economy (place land OR gain mana OR draw - pick one) and how it paces games from land-focused early turns into combat-focused late turns
take_what: Single shared action-economy dial: each turn you choose exactly ONE of {place land, gain mana, draw card} - this forces an explicit early-game tradeoff between board expansion and resource banking, naturally staging games into a land phase then a combat phase without a separate rule needed to enforce it

name: Hive Board Game Strategy Guide - The Gamers Guides
one_line: Beginner-to-intermediate strategy guide covering queen placement, blocking, ant pathing, and endgame surrounds.
take_what: the queen-placement tempo rule: the queen bee MUST be placed by a player's 4th turn at the latest, forcing every opening to resolve its central commitment within a fixed small window instead of drifting

name: Into the Breach: Why I'm so invested in what happens on an 8x8 grid (Cane and Rinse)
one_line: Player essay on why the tiny 8x8 board and perfect information produce chess-like tension
take_what: Board is deliberately tiny (8x8, effectively ~1-3 units per side active at once) so every tile you place or move into is legible at a glance - the fixed small space is what makes 'strategic feeling' readable, contrasted against Limen's larger hex board where influence math is invisible

name: PUBG Blue Zone (Playzone) phase schedule
one_line: Battle royale safe-zone shrinks in 9 discrete phases, each with its own wait time, shrink duration, and DPS (damage per second) outside it, ramping from 0.4 HP/s to lethal.
take_what: Explicit escalating schedule: early phases have long wait+shrink windows and near-zero punishment (phase 1: 120s wait, 300s shrink, 0.4 HP/s), late phases compress to 30-60s windows with severe punishment - the SCHEDULE itself is the pacing tool, not just 'a zone shrinks'
constraint: none - reimplement as rift-seam expansion schedule with turn-count triggers instead of real-time

name: MTG Storm mechanic
one_line: Storm counts every spell cast earlier in the turn and creates that many free copies of the storm spell when it resolves - a mechanic built entirely around a single explosive turn
take_what: a counter that accumulates silently over the course of ONE turn (not the whole game) and pays off at the end of that turn in a single dramatic multiplication - distinct from Landfall's per-action trigger because the payoff is deliberately deferred and stacks invisibly, producing the 'oh no here it comes' tension read by the opponent. For Limen: a rite or capital-adjacent effect that counts tiles placed/captured this turn and multiplies a final effect could create the missing 'wow moment'

name: Yavalath rules and forced-move strategy
one_line: Cameron Browne's machine-evolved connection game: make 4-in-a-row to win, but making 3-in-a-row (without also making 4) is an instant loss - so the real skill is forcing the OPPONENT into an unavoidable 3-in-a-row.
take_what: A self-endangering aggression rule: overextending a formation can trigger your own loss condition, so players must attack via forced moves rather than brute stacking. Applied to Limen: a tile-placement pattern that creates 3+ of your own tiles in an unbroken adjacent line (or ring) without a capital/anchor tile could trigger a small self-penalty (influence drain), forcing players to break their own turtle shapes and reach across the board instead of piling tiles safely.
constraint: none - open rules, would need reskinning to hex-influence math

name: Tak center-control strategy analysis
one_line: Strategy writeup showing why center squares in Tak are worth more than edge/corner squares - center pieces touch 4 neighbors vs 3 (edge) or 2 (corner).
take_what: Adjacency-count asymmetry by board position (center=4 neighbors, edge=3, corner=2) makes center tiles structurally more valuable for any 'influence from neighbors' formula - on a hex grid centers have 6 neighbors vs 3-4 on edges, so an influence-sum mechanic like Limen's already has an implicit center-pull that could be made explicit/telegraphed to players
constraint: none - confirms hex board math already biases toward center fights, may just need better UI signaling

name: Meeple Like Us - Hive (2001) design review
one_line: Accessibility-focused design critique arguing Hive's depth comes entirely from movement constraints stacked on a trivial ruleset, but at a real learnability cost.
take_what: the game separates placement rules (new pieces only touch same color, until turn 2 where they must NOT touch opponent) from movement rules (once queen is down, any legal slide/hop applies) - this placement/movement asymmetry is explicitly credited with avoiding memorized 'book openings' the way chess suffers from
constraint: note the reviewer's warning: this same depth makes new-vs-expert games un-fun, a real risk for Limen's onboarding

name: Shut Up & Sit Down - Hive Mind: How to Win at Hive Like a Master
one_line: Satirical strategy article built around real Hive board states, illustrating beetle-climb encirclement and multi-piece surround threats.
take_what: the beetle's ability to physically stack ON TOP of any piece (friend or foe), taking that hex out of play for movement purposes while itself becoming a mobile 'lid' that can be dropped onto the queen's last open hex from above - a vertical threat vector distinct from lateral siege

name: Road to the IGF: Subset Games' Into the Breach
one_line: Gamasutra/Game Developer interview on IGF entry covering telegraphing, collateral damage and weapon design
take_what: Weapons are valued for side-effects (push/knockback) over raw damage - artillery that shoves a unit into a hazard or into another enemy is rated as more impactful than direct-damage weapons, because it creates a second-order combo the player must plan

name: Multiplayer Solitaire? (BGG Mechanica thread)
one_line: General BGG discourse thread on what makes engine-builders feel like multiplayer solitaire
take_what: Community consensus framing: 'multiplayer solitaire' = each player optimizes their own board/engine without needing to track or respond to what opponents are doing - the diagnostic test is 'could you play this exact same turn if the other player's board were hidden from you?' If yes, it's solitaire
constraint: none - diagnostic heuristic, not a mechanic to port

name: Neuroshima Hex! Strategy blog
one_line: Player-written faction strategy guides covering the Net token and base-adjacency pressure tactics
take_what: A single 'Net' effect token can immobilize/disable an enemy HQ or key unit outright ('netting their base can totally derail' a mobility-dependent faction) - one narrow removal-of-agency card counters an entire faction archetype, creating rock-paper-scissors tension between factions rather than pure stat racing

name: Weekly Vault: XP-scaled chest tier that only ratchets up, never down
one_line: A single chest per week whose tier (and thus loot quality/quantity) increases with weekly XP earned from any mode; explicitly designed to give 'the thrill of pack pulls without making players pay for it'
take_what: one chest, opened once a week, whose CONTENTS scale with a visible meter that only goes up during the week - the open-the-chest moment is the deliberate variable-reward hook, decoupled entirely from spend
constraint: none - this is a pure UX/reward-cadence pattern, no license issue; addresses Limen's 'no addictive hook' problem directly since Limen currently has no meta-progression loop at all

name: Polytopia Fandom Wiki — Strategies (aggressive play, turn-3 second-village benchmark)
one_line: Community strategy pages give hard turn-number benchmarks: capture 2nd village by turn 3, always buy level-2 capital (+1 income) turn 0, land-grab speed beats defense early
take_what: A concrete, teachable pacing benchmark ('by turn N you should have done X') that players can self-check against — gives Limen a diagnosable early-game health metric (e.g. 'by turn 3 you should have made contact/first capture attempt') instead of a vague 'don't turtle' design goal

name: Summoner Wars 2E - First Thoughts review (The Solo Meeple)
one_line: Player review/postmortem of first games, noting event-card timing tricks and the payoff of forward summoner pushes
take_what: reviewer initially played it safe/defensive and found the game punishing - 'defensive play initially seemed more prudent' but forward Summoner+Gate pushes into enemy territory won; also event cards that force a unit to move after attacking read as 'getting an extra move' - a small burst effect that reads as huge because it breaks the expected action economy

name: Summoner Wars event-card summon tricks (Summoning Surge, Forced Summon, Mirage)
one_line: How-to-play breakdown covering the Event Phase and cards that let you summon mid-event, ambushing from unexpected board positions
take_what: a distinct 'Play Events' phase sits between Summon and Movement in the turn order; certain event cards let you summon a SECOND unit during this phase from a wall/gate the opponent didn't expect, creating a one-two ambush inside a single turn - the trick is entirely about phase-order exploitation, not raw card power
constraint: Limen's 3 spell 'rites' could gain a similar phase-order trick: a rite that lets you place a second tile after your normal placement, contingent on already having placed near the rift

name: Dota Underlords positioning guide — Knights cube formation & Drow range (BlueStacks)
one_line: Concrete synergy-shape example: Knights want a literal 3x3 cube block; Drow buffs allies within 1 square
take_what: synergy bonuses tied to a specific GEOMETRIC SHAPE (3x3 block) rather than just 'adjacent count' gives placement a puzzle-piece feel — the player is solving a shape-fitting problem, not just a threshold-counting one
constraint: none — maps cleanly onto Limen's hex tiles as a rare card effect ('bonus if you own all 6 hexes surrounding this tile' i.e. a full ring)

name: Balatro's Cursed Design Problem - Mark Brown / GMTK
one_line: Balatro deliberately hides score previews to create slot-machine suspense, but the math is fully calculable so players spreadsheet around it
take_what: The tension between 'hidden outcome for excitement' and 'fully deterministic math players can precompute' - Limen's influence formula is similarly deterministic (base+adjacent-enemy), so hiding effective-influence numbers to build suspense will just get players to mentally/spreadsheet-calculate it instead; if suspense is wanted, the randomness must be real (card draw order, not math obfuscation)
constraint: none - design lesson, not a mechanic to port

name: Balatro Design Analysis: Visual Packaging (material cue system)
one_line: Cards use material/texture (gold=currency, glass=fragile-high-mult) instead of text to signal mechanical role
take_what: Encode a tile's mechanical property (rift-adjacent/drained, towered, capturable-this-turn) as a material/texture shift on the tile itself (cracked/scorched edge, glow ring at <=0 effective influence) rather than a floating number label - so board state reads at a glance
constraint: needs original art pass, no license issue

name: Level Up / Transform - Legends of Runeterra Wiki
one_line: Champion cards instantly transform into an upgraded permanent form mid-match when a per-card condition is met, with a bespoke on-board animation
take_what: A condition-triggered in-place transform (same unit, new stats/art/animation, persists rest of game) fires automatically the instant the trigger condition is satisfied during any turn, not just on-play - the payoff moment is decoupled from the placement moment, creating a second surprise beat later in the match

name: Marvel Snap Gameplay Design Deconstruction (LinkedIn, Ceeyus Vareed)
one_line: Practitioner breakdown of Snap's simultaneous-turn structure and randomized location reveal timing (locations 1-3 reveal on turns 1-3 respectively)
take_what: Locations are hidden until the turn they're relevant, revealing progressively (turn-1 location visible immediately, turn-3 location hidden until turn 3) so the board's rules change mid-match and force replanning - a staggered information-reveal schedule tied to turn number, not to card draws

name: Faeria - Double Collecting / Well Control (Board Control guide)
one_line: Explains 'double collecting': parking one creature between two adjacent wells to harvest 2 resources/turn instead of 1, making specific board positions objectively more valuable than others
take_what: A small number of fixed high-value board coordinates (wells) that reward a specific placement pattern (adjacency to two of them at once) - creates a contestable landmark on the map that both players fight over early, independent of hand contents

name: Atari (Go term) - GoMagic
one_line: Atari is the state of a stone/group with exactly one liberty left - a direct, unmissable capture threat that forces an immediate opposing response or loss of the group.
take_what: A binary, loudly-telegraphed 'one step from death' state (not a hidden math threshold). Limen's capture rule (effective influence <=0) is currently a quiet number comparison; borrowing atari's UX - a hard visual/audio state change the instant a tile crosses '1 point from capturable' - would make the existing math read as a threat rather than a spreadsheet check, addressing the 'placement lacks strategic feeling' problem without touching the underlying formula.

name: BGDF: Incentivizing Aggressiveness (design forum thread)
one_line: Board Game Designers Forum thread cataloguing concrete mechanisms used across published games to force early player conflict instead of parallel corner-turtling.
take_what: Named mechanisms: (a) maintenance/upkeep economies that punish passive accumulation and force expansion into contested space, (b) territory value that depreciates the longer it's held uncontested (kills 'sit in my corner' as a viable line), (c) risk/reward skew where the first aggressor can claim enough resource lead that non-aggression becomes a losing strategy.
constraint: none - generic design theory, safe to adapt

name: Wingspan solo-vs-multiplayer criticism (Table for ONE review)
one_line: Review naming Wingspan as a 'classic example of multiplayer solitaire' with near-zero cross-player interaction
take_what: Named failure mode: the ONLY interaction point in Wingspan multiplayer is card-sniping (someone takes the bird you wanted from a shared row) - everything else (egg-laying, food, bonus cards) is purely internal to your own tableau. This is the anti-pattern Limen's 'own corner' problem resembles: interaction reduced to a single shared-resource contention point instead of woven through the whole turn

name: King of the Hill board game mechanic overview
one_line: BGG mechanic tag/index for games where occupying a designated hill/hex grants ongoing points or advantage while contested each turn.
take_what: Persistent per-turn scoring tick for holding a specific tile ('king' role re-rolled/contested every turn by whoever occupies it) rather than a one-time capture bonus - converts a single hex into a recurring income stream that both sides must keep fighting over turn after turn
constraint: none - could be a single 'capital-adjacent' hex granting +1 influence/turn to whoever's tile currently occupies it

name: Summoner Wars - UltraBoardGames rules (Master Set / 1E)
one_line: Full rules writeup: 6-phase turn (Draw, Summon, Events, Move, Attack, Build Magic), Magic Pile as deck-as-resource, hard action caps
take_what: hard per-turn caps - move up to 3 units (2 spaces each), attack with up to 3 units - deliberately prevent 'flooding the board and grinding'; separately, Magic is paid by discarding cards straight off your own draw deck (Magic Pile), so every point of mana literally thins your future hand - your deck is simultaneously your card supply and your mana pool
constraint: the deck-as-mana coupling is a strong lever for Limen's 'decks feel thin' problem - it makes a 20-card deck feel weightier because every summon has an opportunity cost against future draws

name: Risk of Rain 2 — Director Coefficient Difficulty Scaling
one_line: Roguelike horde-survival where a global 'coeff' rises with playtime and jumps 15% at every stage-clear, governing what the spawn Director can afford to send at you
take_what: coeff = (playerFactor + minutes*timeFactor) * 1.15^stagesCompleted — a single exponential-ish scalar that both (a) increases enemy budget over time and (b) forces the spawner to stop sending cheap/lone enemies once coeff is high, guaranteeing spawns never trivially decay into nothing
constraint: none - formula shape only, not code

name: Game Design Technique: Collection Sets (Yu-kai Chou)
one_line: Gamification essay on collection-set psychology: optimal set size 7-12 items, 40-60% completion is the tipping point where 'endowed progress' kicks in, final item must be moderately hard not impossible
take_what: cap any single collectible set (e.g. a keyword's card family, a tier of tiles) at 7-12 members and design the last unlock to require real-but-achievable effort - too big a pool (Limen's '~20 card deck feels thin' problem) may actually be the wrong axis; sub-collections of 7-12 give completable arcs inside the larger pool

name: Duelyst pixel-art VFX and animation juice (Glauber Kotaki lead animator)
one_line: Duelyst's reputation for 'making pixel art turn-based CCGs look good' came from small per-unit animation touches: cloth/cape physics, idle breathing, impactful hit-stop on attacks.
take_what: Juice budget spent on a handful of cheap, high-repeat animation beats (idle breathe, attack windup+cape whoosh, hit-stop/screen-shake on capture) rather than spread thin across every card — the same few motions replay hundreds of times per match and are what players remember.

name: UltraBoardGames - Tips to Win Hive
one_line: Short tips page reinforcing queen mobility and multi-threat tactics.
take_what: the 'multiple threat paths' tip: strong players deliberately create two or more simultaneous surround threats on the queen so the opponent's single defensive move can only block one, converting a numeric-advantage board state into a forced win - i.e. design for unavoidable dual-threat forks as the actual close-out mechanism, not raw material lead

name: Dominion attack cards (Witch/Militia/Curse) design intent - Simulate Dominion blog
one_line: Analysis of Dominion's attack-card subsystem, the mechanism most credited with making an otherwise-parallel deckbuilder feel competitive
take_what: Attack cards (Witch gives opponents a dead Curse card that clogs their deck and costs -1VP; Militia forces opponents to discard down to 3 cards) are OPTIONAL cards in the shared market, not baseline rules - so interaction level is a dial the table sets by which market cards get included that game, and a Moat-type reaction card lets a target cancel the attack, creating a rock-paper-scissors tension around whether to invest turns in defense
constraint: Dominion's specific cards are IP; the 'attack cards are optional buy-in, defense is a purchasable counter' pattern is generic

name: Smash Up shared bases
one_line: Card game where N+1 shared 'base' cards sit on the table simultaneously; each base scores independently once total minion power crosses its breakpoint, forcing multi-front conflict every round instead of one long buildup.
take_what: Multiple simultaneous small contested objectives (bases) that each resolve and get REPLACED on their own schedule, rather than one long game-length struggle - guarantees several conflict flashpoints per game instead of a single climax
constraint: none - could map to multiple small 'hot' hexes with bonus influence that periodically relocate

name: How Subset Games made the jump from FTL to Into the Breach (Game Developer)
one_line: Interview on the design pivot from FTL's randomness toward ITB's zero-RNG combat, chasing 'every death feels like my fault'
take_what: Explicit design goal stated as a single sentence test: 'every death should feel like the player's own fault' - used as a filter to cut any mechanic (hidden info, dice-based combat resolution) that let players blame the game instead of their own move; useful inverse-check for Limen's current RNG/draw-based feel

name: Why Race for the Galaxy is definitely not multiplayer solitaire (BGG thread)
one_line: BGG thread defending RftG against the multiplayer-solitaire charge via its simultaneous role-selection system
take_what: Every round all players secretly pick 1 of 7 roles and reveal simultaneously; ALL selected roles fire for EVERYONE that round, but only the player(s) who picked a given role get a bonus on it - so your choice of role is a bet on what your opponents will pick, and picking a role your opponent needs denies them the bonus even though they still get the base action
constraint: role-selection is a genre staple, easy to reimplement as a mechanism not IP

name: Tea for Two - A Neuroshima Hex: Battle Review (Player Elimination)
one_line: Two-player-focused review discussing the swingy, cascading nature of Battle resolution once it triggers
take_what: Battle outcomes are highly variant by design - 'some battles result in a tiny firefight... others are a cascade of carnage' - because instant-action tiles (push, pull, stun) played mid-setup can chain-react through the initiative order and flip which units are even adjacent when resolution starts

name: Region Reward Roads - faction-locked unlock tracks
one_line: Six non-seasonal, permanent per-region reward tracks; playing/winning with a region's cards earns that region's XP, which fills only that region's road toward guaranteed cards - same total rewards regardless of unlock order
take_what: a persistent, never-resetting per-archetype/faction progress bar that's filled ONLY by playing that faction, guaranteeing (not RNG-gating) the next unlock for the archetype you're already committed to - contrast with a shared random pool
constraint: none - directly portable to Limen's deck-thinness problem as a 'play tier-2/3 cards, unlock guaranteed new tier-2/3 cards' track instead of one shared unlock pool

name: Plants vs. Zombies — Flag Zombie Huge Waves
one_line: Lane-defense game whose on-screen progress bar telegraphs periodic 'huge wave' spikes led by a Flag Zombie, roughly every 10th wave, visible to the player in advance
take_what: A visible, always-on progress meter that spikes with a distinct marker (flag icon) BEFORE the huge wave hits, so the player can see the coming crunch and choose to spend resources/set up defense in advance rather than being surprised

name: Corrupt (Hearthstone, Madness at the Darkmoon Faire)
one_line: A card in hand silently transforms into a stronger 'Corrupted' version the instant you play any OTHER card costing more mana than it
take_what: passive in-hand transformation triggered by an unrelated action (playing a bigger card) - the payoff surfaces later as a visible glow/upgrade on a card you're already holding. For Limen's thin-deck problem: cards in hand could silently upgrade based on board state (e.g. a tile card 'corrupts' into a stronger version once you control 3+ tiles), giving a reason to hold and check hand each turn instead of dumping curve-out

name: Faeria - Lands and Land Placement (Fandom wiki)
one_line: Wiki page cataloguing land types, Faeria wells, and the loyalty-cost rule requiring adjacent matching-color land to cast colored cards
take_what: Card color/cost is gated by LOYALTY to adjacent land of the matching type, not by generic mana - so every card played is also a statement about which tiles you've placed nearby, tying deckbuilding identity directly to board geography instead of an abstract resource pool

name: BoardGameArena Hive rules doc
one_line: Canonical digital-implementation rules reference for Hive including sliding and freedom-to-move constraints.
take_what: the 'Freedom to Move' / sliding rule: a piece can only physically slide from one adjacent hex to another if the gap it slides through is wide enough (not pinched between two occupied hexes on both sides) - movement is blocked by geometry, not just occupancy

name: MTG Arena Wildcard progression track
one_line: Every pack opened grants +1 progress on separate Uncommon and Rare/Mythic wildcard tracks; hitting 6 progress auto-grants a wildcard of that rarity, letting players craft any specific card
take_what: Dual-track guaranteed-currency-per-pack-opened (not random) that converts into player-chosen specific card crafts at a fixed progress threshold (6) - removes total bad-luck streaks while still gating behind repeated pack-opening sessions

name: Hearthstone Deck Recipes
one_line: Guided fill-in-the-blank decklists shown in the deckbuilder for new players: pick an archetype, the game auto-suggests remaining slots from owned cards to complete a coherent curve
take_what: A deckbuilder mode that presents partially-filled 'recipe' shells (archetype + curve gaps highlighted) rather than a blank 20-slot grid - turns 'my deck feels thin' into a guided completion task instead of an intimidating empty list

name: Konkr.io
one_line: Free browser hex territory-capture strategy game (Phaser-based, 2025 feature on Phaser.io) inspired by Slay: expand provinces, capture enemy hexes when your unit's strength exceeds every defender's strength.
take_what: Strict strength/threshold capture rule (attacker strength must exceed EVERY defending tile's strength, not just net) plus province-wide income: each connected province earns 1 coin per tile per turn, banked at towns - so bigger stable territory funds more/stronger pushes, creating a snowball that pressures players to contest borders early before opponents outscale them.

name: Splendor rules - shared card row + token pool
one_line: Splendor's shared 4-card-per-tier display and shared communal token pool as the sole interaction surface in an otherwise parallel-building game
take_what: Only 4 cards per tier are ever face-up and purchasable at once, drawn from a shared deck - so a card you're saving up for can be bought out from under you by anyone, anytime, forcing a live threat-read every turn ('do I buy now at a loss, or risk losing the tempo play'). Same for gem tokens: taking 2-of-a-color requires 4+ remaining, so hoarding denies opponents outright
constraint: none - shared-limited-display is a generic mechanism

name: PUBG Playzone wiki - endgame circle behavior
one_line: Detailed breakdown of PUBG's playzone including the final circle-to-zero countdown (180s hold then 15s countdown before the zone shrinks to nothing) guaranteeing a hard endpoint to every match.
take_what: A hard guaranteed endgame timer (final zone always collapses to a single point within a fixed countdown) prevents infinite stalling in the last stretch - Limen's ~20-card deck-out could add an accelerating 'last N turns' rift-expansion so the endgame is forced rather than a slow influence-tally stalemate

name: Kingdom Rush — Wave-based Tower Defense Series
one_line: Classic wave-based tower defense with a manual 'call next wave early' button that lets skilled players compress downtime and stack overlapping waves for bonus rewards
take_what: Giving the player agency to voluntarily overlap/accelerate the next escalation step (rather than a fixed timer) rewards mastery and creates player-driven tempo instead of only designer-driven tempo

name: TFT Positioning Guide (Mobalytics)
one_line: Guide covering frontline/backline layering and AOE-range item interactions in Teamfight Tactics
take_what: asymmetric tank placement: put the TANKIEST unit on the outside edge, not center, because enemy corner-parked carries route damage there first, and a stronger unit soaking the wrong-side attack stalls longer than a weak one would

name: Auto-Battling Your Way to Victory is Not a Good Design (Jeff Witt, Medium/ggDigest)
one_line: Critique essay arguing hands-off autobattle combat removes player agency once positioning/drafting phase ends
take_what: warns that once setup phase ends and combat auto-resolves, players become spectators to their own decisions for the whole fight duration — the 'wow' moment has to land in the SETUP phase itself (placement, draft) since there is no more agency to feel afterward
constraint: directly relevant to Limen's 'no wow moment' problem: since Limen has NO separate auto-resolve combat phase at all (capture is instant on placement), the fix is to make the capture MOMENT itself (the instant a tile flips to <=0 and gets sniped from anywhere) the spectacle beat, not defer juice to a fight animation

name: VFX as a Game Design Language - An-Tim Nguyen, GDC 2022 slides
one_line: Counterplay Games VFX lead's framework for using visual effects to communicate game-design intent (readability, hierarchy, feedback) rather than pure spectacle
take_what: VFX should encode a design signal a player can read at a glance (e.g. color = ownership/threat tier, silhouette = ability type) before it's decoration - suggests Limen's capture/rift/tower states each need one consistent readable VFX grammar, not per-card bespoke effects

name: ISLANDERS - two-choice building-pack unlock at point thresholds
one_line: On hitting a score threshold, player picks ONE of two offered building-pack themes (e.g. farming vs fishing) to unlock next, permanently shaping what's available for the rest of that island
take_what: A binary draft choice at milestones (pick pack A or B) that locks in a build direction - could map to Limen deck construction as a small in-run drafting layer to address 'decks feel thin', letting players branch mid-run rather than only pre-game deckbuild
constraint: changes core deckbuilding model - would need play-testing to see if it fits Limen's fixed 20-card deck format

name: Hearthstone tutorial: scripted unlosable missions with red-arrow guidance
one_line: 58 unique tutorial-only cards, heavily scripted fights the player literally cannot lose, red arrows/highlights/unprompted tooltips pointing at the correct next action each step
take_what: A bespoke, non-replayable tutorial card pool distinct from the real game, paired with forced-correct-play scripting (opponent AI plays into a script) so turn 1 always produces a real board interaction - directly attacks 'combat starts too slow' by hand-scripting the new player's first clash to happen turn 1-2, not turn 6

name: Manahex
one_line: 2024-25 hex-board fantasy TCG (Steam/itch, by Erik Svedäng) for 2-4 players: move your mage onto an adjacent hex to take control of it, and each hex's color/type generates the specific mana used to cast that turn's spells/creatures/buildings.
take_what: Board position IS the resource: controlled hexes generate typed mana on the spot (no separate mana pool/land-drop system), so every tile you place or move onto has an immediate, visible payoff tied to color-matching - collapsing 'build economy' and 'place tile' into one legible action.
constraint: none - mechanism is generic resource-on-tile pattern

name: Reimagining failure in strategy game design in Into the Breach (Game Developer)
one_line: Article on how ITB decouples 'losing a unit' from 'losing the game' via pilot XP carrying forward through timeline resets
take_what: Mech (the placeable unit) is disposable and heals automatically after every battle; the only thing that truly persists and can be permanently lost is the pilot's XP/bonuses riding inside it - this frees players to sacrifice board pieces tactically because the punishment is narrow and specific, not 'you lost your whole board state'
constraint: Limen has no pilot-equivalent yet; would require a new persistent-progression layer separate from tiles

name: Marvel Snap's First Three Explosive Months: The Ben Brode Creator Interview
one_line: Kotaku interview with Ben Brode covering design philosophy, animation pacing, and card power balance
take_what: combo/chain resolutions that would run long auto-fast-forward to the final state instead of playing out step by step, so a big turn never costs real clock time

name: Second Dinner's Ben Brode reveals Marvel Snap's recipe for success
one_line: Mobile Gamer interview on Marvel Snap's design recipe: mashing up Backgammon, simultaneous reveal, ability-locations, and Clash Royale's short match length
take_what: the design was assembled as an explicit recipe of borrowed mechanisms (doubling cube + simultaneous reveal + location abilities + sub-5-minute match length) rather than invented from scratch - a reusable template for combining known-good primitives into a new hybrid

name: They Are Billions — Day/Night Swarm Cycle
one_line: City-builder/tower-defense hybrid alternating calm build-up phases with periodic zombie swarm attacks, culminating in one final overwhelming swarm from all map edges
take_what: Structural rhythm of build-phase -> attack-phase -> build-phase, with each attack phase strictly larger than the last and the final attack an explicit 'everything at once' climax rather than a continuation of gradual scaling

name: Throwing Out the Dopamine Shots: Reward Psychology Without the Neurotrash
one_line: GDC 2017 talk (Ben Lewis-Evans, Epic Games) arguing effective rewards come from variable-ratio schedules, control, and clear feedback/expectation-setting, not neuromyth 'dopamine hits'
take_what: reward schedule should be variable-RATIO (payout tied to actions taken, e.g. captures made) not variable-INTERVAL (tied to time) - for Limen, tie the 'wow' unlock/reward moment to a specific in-match action (first capture, first tower built) rather than a fixed turn count
constraint: paywalled GDC Vault talk, only abstract/summary accessible free

name: Inscryption - How a game jam on 'sacrifices' became Inscryption (Game Developer / Gamasutra)
one_line: Postmortem on Inscryption's origin: sacrifice mechanic (spend N creatures on board to summon a stronger one) came directly from a 48-hour jam theme, later wrapped in ARG horror framing
take_what: Card cost is denominated in board presence, not a resource pool: stronger cards show their cost as literal blood-drop icons equal to the number of your own creatures you must remove from the board to play them, making the tradeoff physically visible on the card face itself
constraint: would require redesigning Limen's influence-cost display; a card-face cost icon is cheap to prototype

name: Slay the Spire GDC talk: Metrics Driven Design and Balance
one_line: Mega Crit's Anthony Giovannetti on using play-metrics (not just feel) to balance a deckbuilder around the 'avalanche' feeling of cards linking together into big combo turns
take_what: design goal stated explicitly: zero in on the feeling of cards CHAINING within a single turn (relic + card synergy producing a cascading damage/defense burst), then use win-rate/pick-rate telemetry per card to find which combo pieces are underused and undertuned rather than guessing. For Limen: instrument which tile/rite combos actually get chained in real games and buff the ones with high 'combo satisfaction' but low pick rate
constraint: needs telemetry infra Limen may not have yet

name: Ladder (Go) - Wikipedia
one_line: A ladder is a forced zigzag capture sequence: each atari (capture threat) forces exactly one legal response, so the whole sequence is calculable from the first move, and whether a 'ladder breaker' stone exists elsewhere on the board changes the correct move dozens of tiles away.
take_what: The 'ladder breaker' concept: a single stone placed far from the current fight can retroactively make a forced sequence favorable or unfavorable, meaning good players read board-wide interactions before starting a local fight. For Limen, this suggests exposing an 'if I place here, does it set up an inevitable capture chain elsewhere' preview/highlight - not a rules change but a UI/legibility feature that makes the existing influence math feel spatial and forward-looking rather than purely local arithmetic.

name: Board Game Design Day: "King Me" - A Defense of King-Making (GDC Vault)
one_line: GDC talk defending king-making (a losing player's choice deciding who wins) as a legitimate, even desirable, interaction mechanism rather than a bug to design out
take_what: Reframes 'kingmaking' - normally considered a flaw - as evidence a game has REAL interaction: if a losing player's final moves can swing the outcome between two leaders, every player's position matters to every other player until the very end, which is the opposite of parallel solitaire play where only your own score matters
constraint: talk video, not fully transcribed by fetch - treat as pointer for deeper viewing

name: Forbidden Island - shrinking board via tile removal
one_line: Cooperative game where flood cards flip tiles face-down then remove them entirely, physically shrinking the playable island and forcing players to route around a hole that grows every round.
take_what: Two-stage removal: a tile is first FLOODED (warning state, still usable but marked) before it's fully SUNK (removed) - gives players one round of advance warning before a hex becomes permanently unusable, which Limen's rift-seam mechanic could borrow for hazard tiles that telegraph before draining/removing adjacent tiles
constraint: none - Limen is competitive not co-op, but the two-stage warning-then-removal pattern transfers to hazard escalation

name: MTG Arena pack-opening reveal sequence
one_line: GDC talk breakdown of MTGA's card pack reveal: 8 cards flip on click, revealed in ascending rarity order (commons first, rare/mythic last)
take_what: click-to-reveal one card at a time, sorted so rarity climbs toward the end - guarantees the LAST card of any reveal sequence is the best one seen, so anticipation compounds instead of front-loading the payoff
constraint: none - pure UI sequencing pattern, no license issue

name: Duelyst open-source revival (OpenDuelyst / Duelyst 2)
one_line: Counterplay released full Duelyst source + assets royalty-free in 2023; a fan team (Duelyst 2) got a license and relaunched it in Dec 2022 with community-driven balance patches.
take_what: Concrete, inspectable reference implementation of the mana-tile/general/replace systems (actual code, not just rules text) — usable as a direct implementation reference for tile-adjacency and turn-economy logic if Limen's team wants to check exact numbers/edge cases rather than reconstruct from wiki text.

name: Stately Play review of Race for the Galaxy
one_line: Review that names RftG's low-interaction reputation directly and frames it as a design-philosophy tradeoff (racing to build vs. attacking)
take_what: Reviewer's framing that a game can be legitimately low-interaction if it fully commits to being a RACE (relative standing matters, not board presence) - names the exact tension Limen is trying to avoid: 'racing to build the best engine rather than blowing each other up'

name: Pity timers explained (soft/hard pity)
one_line: Breakdown of pity-timer math across Hearthstone (guaranteed legendary within 40 packs), Diablo 3 (rising legendary odds the longer you go without one) and Dota 2 rigged crits
take_what: a counter tracks 'draws since X', and probability of X rises (soft pity) or hits 100% at a hard cap (hard pity) - caps worst-case variance without removing randomness's excitement

name: MTG Arena Daily Wins reward curve
one_line: MTGA's per-win daily reward table: win 1 = 250 gold, wins 2-4 = 100 gold each, then alternating card rewards and diminishing gold (50g, 25g) through win 15
take_what: steeply front-loaded per-session reward curve (first win worth 2.5x the next three, tapering hard after) - creates a strong 'get my first win in' session-start hook and a soft stop signal after ~4 wins so players feel fine quitting instead of burning out

name: Carcassonne field-scoring completed-city-count (not tile-count) mechanic
one_line: Farm scoring counts the number of COMPLETED cities bordering the field (3pts each), not the farm's tile area - so a small farm touching 3 finished cities beats a huge farm touching one
take_what: Score a zone by the count of qualifying adjacent COMPLETED structures rather than by raw tile area - rewards positioning near multiple finished assets over sheer size, and creates a race to finish structures before a farm 'locks in' its score
constraint: would require Limen to define a 'completed structure' concept it currently lacks (towers/tiles are individually scored via influence, not grouped structures)

name: Golden card - Hearthstone Wiki (wiki.gg)
one_line: Cosmetic-tier card variant: gold frame + unique per-card animation, deliberately harder to get on weak/basic cards to make the drop feel earned
take_what: Rarity-gated animation tier (every card has a base version; a golden/foil version plays a bespoke idle+play animation) rewards specific achievement thresholds (e.g. win counts) rather than random pack luck for basic cards - creates a collectible 'upgrade path' independent of power level
constraint: needs a per-tile animation budget; scope small (recolor + particle trail) if adopted

name: A Taxonomy of Collectible Card Games from a Game-Playing AI Perspective
one_line: Academic taxonomy comparing mechanical structures (resource systems, board topology, hidden information) across major CCGs including Hearthstone, MTG, Gwent, Legends of Runeterra
take_what: a structural framework for classifying WHY interaction timing varies across CCGs (turn-based exclusive vs simultaneous vs reactive/instant-speed) - useful lateral reference for diagnosing Limen's 'combat starts too slowly' problem as a timing-structure issue rather than a numbers-tuning issue: games with reactive/instant-speed interaction (MTG) create earlier tension than strict-alternating games
constraint: academic paper, dense - skim for taxonomy table only

name: UltraBoardGames - Additional Hive Pieces reference
one_line: Reference page detailing Mosquito ability-copying rules and Ladybug's 2-over-1-under movement.
take_what: the Ladybug's fixed movement: exactly 2 steps across the top of the hive then 1 step down to an empty hex touching the hive - a piece whose power is entirely defined by a rigid movement PATTERN rather than a stat, letting it slip behind enemy lines predictably enough to plan around but flexibly enough to surprise

name: Hearthstone legendary pity timer
one_line: Guaranteed legendary within first 10 packs of a new set; guaranteed legendary within 40 packs since your last legendary in that set, counter increments per-set not globally
take_what: A rolling 'pity counter' with escalating draw probability the longer a rarity tier goes un-hit, reset only when that tier hits - guarantees the 'wow' big-card moment on a bounded schedule instead of leaving it to raw variance

name: Hearthstone ranked ladder: Star Bonus + rank floors
one_line: 5 leagues x 10 ranks, 3 stars per rank; Star Bonus multiplies stars earned per win based on prior-season MMR/rank; rank floors at rank 10 and rank 5 prevent demotion below those checkpoints
take_what: Two concrete numbers to steal: (a) floor ranks that make a loss streak non-punishing below a checkpoint, removing ladder-anxiety churn, and (b) a bonus-star multiplier that front-loads fast climbing early in a season so players who return after time away catch up quickly instead of feeling behind

name: ShoreTiles
one_line: 2026 PC tile-placement strategy game with a day/night cycle: build and place tiles freely by day, then at night the sea turns hostile and creatures converge on your lighthouse, forcing defensive tile layout under time pressure.
take_what: Alternating build-phase/threat-phase rhythm plus a permanent-decision rule (no undo on tile placement) that makes every placement feel weighty; the night phase is the 'wow moment' - passive building suddenly becomes a visible, escalating attack wave that tests your layout.
constraint: none - single-player PvE pattern, would need reimagining for 1v1

name: Neuroshima Hex! armies abilities wiki (BoardGameGeek)
one_line: Community-maintained catalog of per-faction unit abilities and initiative spreads
take_what: Faction identity is legible from initiative-value distribution alone (Borgo mutants skew high-initiative/aggressive melee, Moloch skews low-initiative/heavy-armor defensive) - a player can read an opposing deck's temperament from a single stat axis without reading every card

name: Bloons TD 6 — Round Escalation and MOAB-class Spike Rounds
one_line: Tower defense where round difficulty escalates from single weak bloons (round 1) to camo/lead/regrow MOAB-class bosses by round 40, with named spike rounds forcing tower repositioning
take_what: Escalation isn't smooth — specific 'spike rounds' introduce a wholly new threat property (camo, lead, regrow) that invalidates the player's current setup and forces an active response, not just 'bigger numbers'

name: Evolve (MTG, Gatecrash/Simic)
one_line: Whenever you play a NEW creature with higher power or toughness than this one, this one gets a permanent +1/+1 counter - triggers off board development you were doing anyway
take_what: independent-stat comparison (power OR toughness, not both) makes the trigger fire more often than expected, which is why it 'felt' generous - a cheap tuning lever (OR vs AND threshold) that changes trigger frequency without changing the visible rule text much. Relevant to tuning how often Limen's adjacency/influence bonuses proc so board growth feels frequent rather than rare

name: Faeria (Wikipedia)
one_line: Overview confirming the hex 'living board' concept: players build the terrain each turn from an empty map with orbs on opposite corners and four wells scattered near the edges
take_what: Fixed asymmetric well placement (4 wells, off-center, not adjacent to either player's start) guarantees contested neutral ground exists on every map regardless of deck, giving low-skill players an obvious early objective beyond 'build toward the enemy'

name: MTG Arena Mastery Pass (seasonal battle pass)
one_line: ~100-level seasonal XP track tied to each new card set; XP from daily quests + wins + events; free track and paid track run in parallel, both grant packs/cosmetics/gold
take_what: Coupling the battle-pass level track to the SAME cadence as new-card-set releases (not a separate calendar) so 'grinding levels' and 'chasing new cards' are the same activity loop - avoids splitting player attention across two unrelated progression systems
constraint: none - avoid literal paid-track monetization copy if Limen has no IAP model yet

name: Balatro's Card Movements & Shaders Recreated in Unity - 80.lv
one_line: Pointer to André Cardoso's technical breakdown of Balatro's card-separation logic, gameplay wiring, and shaders in a Unity recreation
take_what: Card movement uses simulated inertia that pushes adjacent cards out of the way with magnetic snapping when reordering hand - the hand never has 'dead' static cards, everything visibly reacts to any single card's movement

name: How Priority Works in Marvel SNAP
one_line: Wiki explainer on Marvel Snap's Priority system: who reveals cards first each turn
take_what: priority (who resolves first) is determined dynamically each turn by who is winning more locations, tie-broken by point differential, then coin flip - so board state itself decides turn-order advantage, and specific cards are designed to be strong specifically when you hold or lack priority
constraint: Limen is a live turn-based board not simultaneous reveal, so priority-as-mechanic doesn't map directly, but the underlying idea (being ahead grants an initiative advantage that snowballs) is portable to placement order or first-capture-rights

name: Duelyst shutdown coverage — player base decline, no design postmortem
one_line: Duelyst shut down Feb 2020 after Steam concurrent players fell under ~100/day; publisher Bandai Namco stopped supporting patches, and no official design postmortem was ever published.
take_what: Business/retention lesson only (not a mechanic): a mechanically deep tactics-CCG can still die from lack of onboarding/marketing momentum and publisher abandonment — depth alone didn't retain players. Low direct mechanic-transfer, but useful cautionary context for 'addictive hook' problem: mechanical depth without a compelling early hook or content cadence bleeds players regardless of quality.

name: Legends of Runeterra weekly $13/half-deck spend cap
one_line: Deconstructor of Fun's design breakdown showing Riot hard-caps weekly card purchases to ~18 cards (3 champions max) for ~$13-14, even if you dump $100 into the wallet at once
take_what: a hard weekly purchase/unlock cap decoupled from how much currency a player holds - the cap is on RATE of acquisition, not on wallet size, forcing deckbuilding to unfold over weeks regardless of spend
constraint: Limen has no monetization layer yet, but the underlying mechanism (rate-capped unlocks that pace collection growth week over week) is reusable for a card-unlock/deck-thickening system independent of money

name: Why LoR underperformed: complexity + high skill floor alienated casuals
one_line: Analysis piece arguing LoR's commercial failure stemmed less from its economy and more from a high skill barrier (round-based reactive combat, mana curve tricks) that made it feel like 'work' next to Hearthstone's simpler turns
take_what: the causal claim that generosity alone doesn't retain players if the CORE LOOP itself has too high a cognitive floor per turn - economy generosity can't compensate for a game that feels effortful to just play, which is closer to Limen's actual stated problems (slow starts, unclear tile-placement feel) than the economy per se
constraint: none - directional lesson only, not a mechanism; low novelty but flags that Limen's four stated problems (slow combat start, placement feel, no hook, thin decks) may matter more than any economy fix would

name: Genshin Impact Wish pity system
one_line: Wiki-guide breakdown of Genshin's banner pity: soft pity ramps 5-star odds starting pull 74, hard pity guarantees a 5-star by pull 90, plus a 50/50 coin-flip on which 5-star with a guarantee-next-time loss protection
take_what: the 50/50-with-guaranteed-makeup-next-time structure - losing the coin flip still feels like progress because the NEXT rare pull is locked in; translatable as 'losing a close capture fight still banks a token toward a guaranteed future swing' rather than pure whiff

name: Super Auto Pets Strategies Wiki
one_line: Line-based (not grid) autobattler where front/back slot order alone drives all combat resolution
take_what: positioning collapses to a single ordered line (5 slots) instead of 2D grid, and specific slot numbers (front=tankiest, slot 5=summon-on-faint/buff units) carry fixed roles — proves a much simpler 1D positioning space can still generate deep strategy

name: MTG Arena reward drop rates page

name: How does priority work in Marvel Snap? (Shacknews)
